title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
夫子聖者與何其多能也子貢曰固天縱
之將聖又多能也子聞之曰大宰知我
乎吾少也賤故多能鄙事君子多乎哉
不多也
金輝漢
同考試官教諭單批孔子之聖不在多能此作
理明意盡皆本色語宜錄以式
===
考試官教諭朱批發揮明淨
考試官教授李批精瑩透徹
聖人因人兩擬以聖而執藝以示其意焉夫聖
非藝之可名也大宰昧而不知賢者知而未盡
聖人述所能以示其意也有以哉且夫聖者道
之至而天所成也能者道之緒而聖所該也大
宰徒見聖之能而不見聖之聖故問於子貢曰
夫子聖者與何其多能也執聞見之知而疑聖
之得名者在是淺之乎觀聖矣子貢則見聖之
punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

「夫子聖者與？何其多能也！」子貢曰：「固天縱之將聖，又多能也。」子聞之，曰：「大宰知我乎！吾少也賤，故多能鄙事。君子多乎哉？不多也。」

金輝漢

同考試官教諭單批：孔子之聖，不在多能。此作理明意盡，皆本色語，宜錄以式。
考試官教諭朱批：發揮明淨。
考試官教授李批：精瑩透徹。

聖人因人兩擬以聖，而執藝以示其意焉。夫聖，非藝之可名也。大宰昧而不知，賢者知而未盡，聖人述所能以示其意也，有以哉！且夫聖者，道之至而天所成也；能者，道之緒而聖所該也。大宰徒見聖之能，而不見聖之聖，故問於子貢曰：「夫子聖者與？何其多能也！」執聞見之知，而疑聖之得名者在是，淺之乎觀聖矣！子貢則見聖之
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

"Is the Master a sage? How is it that he has so many abilities?" Zigong 子貢 said, "Indeed, Heaven has endowed him without limit to be a great sage, and moreover he has many abilities." The Master heard of it and said, "Does the Grand宰 (Taizai 大宰) know me? When I was young, my station was humble, and so I acquired many abilities in menial matters. Does the gentleman need to have many abilities? No, he does not need many."

Jin Huihan 金輝漢

Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies (jiaoyu 教諭) Shan 單: The sagehood of Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) does not lie in having many abilities. In this essay, the principles are clear and the meaning is fully expressed; all of it is written in the authentic style of the genre, and it ought to be recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhu 朱: The elaboration is clear and clean.
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies (jiaoshou 教授) Li 李: Refined, lustrous, and thoroughly penetrating.

Because two men both likened him to a sage, the Sage held strictly to his practical arts in order to reveal his true meaning. Now, sagehood is not something that can be named on the basis of practical arts. The Grand宰 was benighted and did not understand this, while the worthy understood it yet not completely; thus, when the Sage recounted the source of his abilities to reveal his true meaning, there was good reason indeed! Moreover, sagehood is the ultimate perfection of the Way, brought to completion by Heaven; ability is a mere byproduct of the Way, encompassed within sagehood. The Grand宰 merely saw the Sage's abilities without seeing the Sage's sagehood, and therefore he asked Zigong: "Is the Master a sage? How is it that he has so many abilities?" Clinging to knowledge derived from what is heard and seen, and suspecting that the reason a sage earns his name lies therein—how shallow was his view of the Sage! Zigong, on the other hand, saw the Sage's…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
聖而亦見聖之能故告於大宰曰固天縱之將
聖又多能也本聰明之盡而意藝之兼能者在
是智足以知聖矣然聖則孔子不居也多能亦
非君子所尚也夫子乃聞而嘆曰世莫我知也
已大宰其知我乎我之多能非如賜之所謂天
縱而無不能也吾少也賤未獲効用于當時多
能鄙事因以博習于名物耳夫君子豈其能之
多云乎哉守吾心之體要不徇象以弊其精神
執天下之易簡不徧物以窮其耳目道本至一
===
君子亦一之而已吾方學君子而未能焉若謂
之聖則豈敢哉是知聖者德也多能藝也德成
而藝自涵焉局于藝矣即無所不能不過竊君
子之餘德者本也藝者末也本立而末自裕焉
得其本矣即有所未能亦不失君子之實夫子
直述已之多能而推不多于君子厥旨深哉噫
德藝一理也博約一事也博而寡要是無本也
逐藝遺德是玩物也不然周公稱才美畢公勤
小物寧獨藝乎哉無言之訓一貫之傳學者合
punctuated: 聖，而亦見聖之能，故告於大宰曰：「固天縱之將聖，又多能也。」本聰明之盡，而意藝之兼能者在是，智足以知聖矣。然聖則孔子不居也，多能亦非君子所尚也。夫子乃聞而嘆曰：「世莫我知也已！大宰其知我乎？我之多能，非如賜之所謂天縱而無不能也。吾少也賤，未獲効用于當時，多能鄙事，因以博習于名物耳。夫君子豈其能之多云乎哉？守吾心之體要，不徇象以弊其精神；執天下之易簡，不徧物以窮其耳目。道本至一，君子亦一之而已。吾方學君子而未能焉，若謂之聖，則豈敢哉？」是知聖者，德也；多能，藝也。德成而藝自涵焉；局于藝矣，即無所不能，不過竊君子之餘。德者，本也；藝者，末也。本立而末自裕焉；得其本矣，即有所未能，亦不失君子之實。夫子直述已之多能，而推不多于君子，厥旨深哉！噫！德藝一理也，博約一事也。博而寡要，是無本也；逐藝遺德，是玩物也。不然，周公稱才美，畢公勤小物，寧獨藝乎哉？無言之訓、一貫之傳，學者合
translation_en: … sagehood, while also seeing the sage's abilities. Therefore, he replied to the Grand宰 (Taizai): "Indeed, Heaven has endowed him comprehensively to be a great sage, and moreover he has many abilities." Grounding it in the perfection of innate intelligence and understanding that his comprehensive mastery of the arts derived from this, Zigong's wisdom was sufficient to know the sage. Yet sagehood was something Confucius would not claim for himself, and having many abilities was likewise not what a superior man esteems. Hearing of this, the Master sighed and said: "No one in the world truly knows me! Does the Grand宰 know me? My having many abilities is not what Ci [Zigong] calls being endowed by Heaven so that there is nothing I cannot do. When I was young, I was of humble station and unable to be of service to my age; thus I became skilled in many menial matters, thereby practicing broadly among names and things. As for the superior man, does he require such a multitude of abilities? He guards the essential substance of his mind and does not wear out his spirit by chasing after outward phenomena; he holds fast to the ease and simplicity of the world and does not exhaust his eyes and ears by trying to cover every object. The Way is fundamentally supreme unity, and the superior man simply unifies himself with it. I am just now striving to learn to be a superior man and have not yet succeeded; if one calls me a sage, how could I dare accept?" From this we know that sagehood is virtue, whereas having many abilities is technical art. When virtue is perfected, the arts are naturally encompassed within it; if one is confined to the arts, even if there is nothing one cannot do, one merely appropriates the leftovers of the superior man. Virtue is the root, and the arts are the branches. When the root is established, the branches naturally flourish; once one attains the root, even if there are things one cannot do, one does not lose the reality of being a superior man. The Master frankly recounted his own many abilities while attributing no need for many abilities to the superior man—how profound was his meaning! Alas! Virtue and the arts are of one principle; breadth of learning and essential restraint are one matter. To be broad in learning yet lacking in essentials is to have no root; to pursue the arts while neglecting virtue is to dally with things. Otherwise, when the Duke of Zhou (Zhougong) was praised for his fine talents, and the Duke of Bi (Bigong) was diligent in small matters, was that merely technical art? The teaching without words and the transmission of the single thread—if scholars bring them together…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而觀之孔門傳受心法可識矣
郊社之禮所以事上帝也
陳貴科
同考試官教諭梁批因郊社以明達孝措語不
繁而意義融貫傑作也
考試官教諭朱批體認精到
考試官教授李批筆力雄渾
觀聖人之所以享帝而制禮之精見矣夫惟仁
人為能享帝也禮行於郊社而上帝所由享焉
===
其義不既精乎中庸賛武周之達孝蓋曰聖人
之制禮也其用意也遠故其取義也精我觀周
禮而知武周之為達孝也已何則迎陽氣之始
復而升中于天禮行于郊也泰壇之奉非徒將
享之彌文而已順陰氣之始萌而告虔于澤禮
行于社也泰折之舉非徒裸獻之飾節而已然
其義何居乃所以事上帝耳體辨於兩儀而祭
以時行將以報其施生之德制隆於昭代而禮
緣義起用以酬其廣大之功司覆司載本至尊
punctuated:
而觀之，孔門傳受心法可識矣。

郊社之禮，所以事上帝也。
陳貴科
同考試官教諭梁批：因郊社以明達孝，措語不繁，而意義融貫，傑作也。
考試官教諭朱批：體認精到。
考試官教授李批：筆力雄渾。

觀聖人之所以享帝，而制禮之精見矣。夫惟仁人為能享帝也，禮行於郊社，而上帝所由享焉，其義不既精乎？《中庸》賛武、周之達孝，蓋曰：聖人之制禮也，其用意也遠，故其取義也精。我觀周禮，而知武、周之為達孝也已。何則？迎陽氣之始復而升中于天，禮行于郊也；泰壇之奉，非徒將享之彌文而已。順陰氣之始萌而告虔于澤，禮行于社也；泰折之舉，非徒裸獻之飾節而已。然其義何居？乃所以事上帝耳。體辨於兩儀，而祭以時行，將以報其施生之德；制隆於昭代，而禮緣義起，用以酬其廣大之功。司覆司載，本至尊
translation_en:
… and examine them together, the mind-method transmitted within the Confucian school can be understood.

"By the ceremonies of the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, they served the Lord on High."
By Chen Guike 陳貴科.
Associate Examiner, Instructor Liang 梁 comments: Using the suburban and altar sacrifices to illuminate far-reaching filial piety, the wording is not verbose yet the meaning is thoroughly integrated; it is a masterpiece.
Examiner, Instructor Zhu 朱 comments: His personal comprehension is precise and thorough.
Examiner, Instructor Li 李 comments: The vigor of his brush is powerful and grand.

When we observe that by which the sages made offerings to the Lord, the subtlety of their institution of rites becomes manifest. Now, only a humane person is able to make offerings to the Lord. When rites are performed at the suburban and earth altars, and the Lord on High thereby receives the offerings, is not the meaning most subtle? When the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) praises the far-reaching filial piety of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, it says in effect: In instituting rites, the sages' intentions were far-reaching, and therefore the meanings they drew were subtle. When I observe the rites of Zhou, I know indeed that King Wu and the Duke of Zhou possessed far-reaching filial piety. Why is this so? Welcoming the initial return of the yang vital force and presenting the burnt offering to Heaven is the rite performed at the suburban altar; the service at the Great Mound (Taitan) is not merely the elaborate ornament of presenting offerings. Following the initial sprouting of the yin vital force and announcing reverence at the marsh is the rite performed at the altar of the soil; the ceremony at the Great Square Pit (Taizhe) is not merely the decorative formality of libations and presentations. Yet wherein does their meaning reside? They are simply the means by which to serve the Lord on High. Their forms are distinguished according to the Two Modes [Heaven and Earth], and the sacrifices are performed according to the seasons, in order to repay Their virtue in bestowing life; the institutions are exalted in an illustrious age, and the rites arise from righteousness, in order to requite Their vast and great achievement. Presiding over the canopy [of Heaven] and presiding over the support [of Earth], They are originally supremely venerable…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而無尚也然元后萬民之父母其位有相爲對
越者夫是以明禋舉焉而上帝是祗禮自不嫌
于僭矣惟玄惟默若至幽而難假也然大君天
地之宗子其氣有相爲流通者夫是以殷薦行
焉而上帝是皇禮自不病其瀆矣是蓋本事親
之心因推之爲事天之典所謂享帝之仁人者
在是即事天之仁益顯其爲事親之孝所謂純
天之翼子者在是我周郊社之禮而豈徒哉吁
聖人制作之精也如此謂之達孝固宜抑有虞
===
氏禘黃帝而郊嚳則郊社之禮自古志之矣夫
子何亟稱于周耶蓋尊尊親親周道大備而達
孝錫類非武周繼述之善未能也先儒有曰舜
爲人道之極萬世仰之不可加周爲王制之備
萬世由之莫能易信哉
聖人人倫之至也欲爲君盡君道欲爲臣
盡臣道二者皆法堯舜而已矣
孫夢熊
同考試官教諭劉批筆力簡勁講法堯舜處尤
punctuated:
而無尚也。然元后萬民之父母，其位有相爲對越者，夫是以明禋舉焉而上帝是祗，禮自不嫌于僭矣。惟玄惟默，若至幽而難假也。然大君天地之宗子，其氣有相爲流通者，夫是以殷薦行焉而上帝是皇，禮自不病其瀆矣。是蓋本事親之心，因推之爲事天之典，所謂「享帝之仁人」者在是；即事天之仁，益顯其爲事親之孝，所謂「純天之翼子」者在是。我周郊社之禮，而豈徒哉？吁！聖人制作之精也如此，謂之達孝固宜。抑有虞氏禘黃帝而郊嚳，則郊社之禮自古志之矣，夫子何亟稱于周耶？蓋尊尊親親，周道大備，而達孝錫類，非武周繼述之善未能也。先儒有曰：「舜爲人道之極，萬世仰之不可加；周爲王制之備，萬世由之莫能易。」信哉！

聖人人倫之至也。欲爲君盡君道，欲爲臣盡臣道，二者皆法堯、舜而已矣。

孫夢熊
同考試官教諭劉批：筆力簡勁，講「法堯舜」處尤
translation_en:
… and unsurpassed. Yet the sovereign is the father and mother of the myriad people, and his position corresponds as a counterpart to that of Heaven and Earth; therefore, when the pure sacrifice is offered to show reverence to the Lord on High, the ritual is naturally free from any suspicion of usurpation. Profound and silent, Heaven and Earth seem utterly abstruse and difficult to reach. Yet the great ruler is the eldest son of Heaven and Earth, and his vital energy circulates in communion with theirs; therefore, when the grand offering is performed to glorify the Lord on High, the ritual is naturally free from the fault of irreverence. This is because, taking root in the heart that serves one's parents, one extends it to become the canon for serving Heaven—this is what is meant by "the humane man who sacrifices to the Lord"; and through the humanity of serving Heaven, one further manifests the filial piety of serving one's parents—this is what is meant by "the reverent son who is pure before Heaven." Could the suburban and altar sacrifices of our Zhou dynasty have been instituted in vain? Ah! Such is the subtlety of the sages' institutions; to call it far-reaching filial piety is fitting indeed. Yet the Lord of Yu performed the ancestral sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor and the suburban sacrifice to Ku, so the rites of the suburban and altar sacrifices had been recorded since antiquity. Why then did the Master so frequently praise the Zhou? It is because in honoring the honorable and loving one's kin, the Way of Zhou was completely realized, and the extension of far-reaching filial piety to all of one's kind could not have been achieved without the excellence of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou in continuing and carrying forward their predecessors' work. Earlier Confucians had a saying: "Shun was the ultimate standard of the human way, whom ten thousand generations look up to without being able to add anything; Zhou was the perfection of kingly institutions, which ten thousand generations follow without being able to alter." Truly it is so!

"The sage is the culmination of human relationships. Whether one wishes to be a ruler and fulfill the way of a ruler, or wishes to be a minister and fulfill the way of a minister, in both cases one need only model oneself on Yao and Shun."

Sun Mengxiong 孫夢熊
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Liu 劉: The brushwork is concise and vigorous; the exposition of "modeling oneself on Yao and Shun" is especially …

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭朱批〔得本旨取之洗盡塵語〕
考試官教授李批〔詞明理順〕
大賢論惟聖盡倫而因舉君臣所當法者焉夫
倫盡於聖而堯舜君臣之極也然則欲盡道者
舍是其奚法哉孟子勉當時之意若曰立人之
道莫大於倫盡倫之極莫過於聖蓋天敘有典
本斯民所共由也然由之而未盡者不可以言
至矣聖人者智本夙成一心而契天經地義之
===
懿德由天縱一身而會民彝物則之全本達德
以行乎達道析之極其精也而天下之軌範立
於此矣由至誠以經綸大經合之盡其大也而
萬世之標準建於此矣是其盡倫也誠無異於
規矩之盡物也而有志於惇倫者將安所取法
哉是故上焉者有君道當盡也如知爲君之難
而欲盡其道亦法堯而已矣下焉者有臣道當
盡也如知爲臣之不易而欲盡其道亦法舜而
已矣爲平章爲協和大哉堯之爲君也萬世稱
punctuated:
考試官教諭朱批：〔得本旨，取之。洗盡塵語。〕
考試官教授李批：〔詞明理順。〕

大賢論惟聖盡倫，而因舉君臣所當法者焉。夫倫盡於聖，而堯、舜君臣之極也，然則欲盡道者，舍是其奚法哉？孟子勉當時之意若曰：立人之道，莫大於倫；盡倫之極，莫過於聖。蓋天敘有典，本斯民所共由也，然由之而未盡者，不可以言至矣。聖人者，智本夙成，一心而契天經地義之懿；德由天縱，一身而會民彝物則之全。本達德以行乎達道，析之極其精也，而天下之軌範立於此矣；由至誠以經綸大經，合之盡其大也，而萬世之標準建於此矣。是其盡倫也，誠無異於規矩之盡物也，而有志於惇倫者，將安所取法哉？是故上焉者，有君道當盡也，如知爲君之難，而欲盡其道，亦法堯而已矣；下焉者，有臣道當盡也，如知爲臣之不易，而欲盡其道，亦法舜而已矣。爲平章，爲協和，大哉堯之爲君也，萬世稱
translation_en:
Examiner Instructor Zhu's comment: [Grasps the fundamental purport; selected. Washes away all hackneyed expressions.]
Examiner Professor Li's comment: [The diction is clear and the reasoning is coherent.]

The great worthy discusses how only the sage fulfills human relationships to the utmost, and therefore cites whom rulers and ministers ought to take as their models. Now, human relationships are fulfilled to the utmost in the sage, and Yao and Shun represent the ultimate standard for rulers and ministers; this being so, for those who wish to fulfill the Way to the utmost, if they set these aside, whom else could they take as a model?

Mencius's intent in exhorting his contemporaries was as if to say: In establishing the Way of humanity, nothing is greater than human relationships; in fulfilling human relationships to the utmost, none surpasses the sage. Indeed, the five cardinal relationships ordained by Heaven are originally what this people jointly follow; yet those who follow them without fulfilling them completely cannot be said to have reached the ultimate. As for the sage, his wisdom is inherently perfected early on, and with a single mind he accords with the excellence of Heaven's invariable principles and Earth's righteous norms; his virtue is endowed by Heaven without limit, and in his single person he embodies the entirety of the people's constant nature and the principles of all things. Grounded in universal virtues to practice the universal Way, when analyzed in detail it reaches the utmost subtlety, and the model for all under Heaven is established herein; proceeding from utmost sincerity to order the great invariable relations of mankind, when synthesized as a whole it exhausts the utmost greatness, and the standard for ten thousand generations is erected herein. Thus, his complete fulfillment of human relationships is truly no different from the compass and carpenter's square completely regulating all things—so where else shall those who aspire to earnestly uphold human relationships take their model?

Therefore, for those above, there is the Way of the ruler that ought to be fulfilled; if one knows the difficulty of being a ruler and wishes to fulfill that Way to the utmost, one should simply model oneself on Yao, and that is all. For those below, there is the Way of the minister that ought to be fulfilled; if one knows that being a minister is not easy and wishes to fulfill that Way to the utmost, one should simply model oneself on Shun, and that is all. Regulating and distinguishing the百官 [clans/officials] and harmonizing the myriad states—great indeed was Yao as a ruler! Ten thousand generations praise…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎授李批通篇剴切讀之凛然
二聖於壯爻與其事之善而原其心之純焉夫
處壯莫善於貞而中其本也九二以之宜二聖
交發其義與且君子之處壯非正無以保其盛
非中無以裕其原卦之九二居陰失正而所處
得中是故周公係爻慮其有用壯之失也而戒
以貞吉焉蓋大壯利貞時則然也故當其時者
不可以過壯也是必以天下之公理行天下之
公事動有關于君德則爲之而弗過于激也政
===
有裨于民瘼則爲之而弗失于驟也觀其所發
一天地正大之情焉惟正可以懾羣邪而彼之
伺隙乘釁者皆不得撓吾剛動之謀矣此正道
行而吉之所以大來乎孔子傳象本其有得正
之心也而原其以中焉蓋因中求正理則然也
故事之正者不容以襲取也由其以天下之公
道秉天下之公心上攄其忠以格君之心爲心
也下宣其猷以惠民之心爲心也察其所存一
天地受中之懿焉惟中可以貫萬事而措之行
punctuated:
考試官敎授李批：通篇剴切，讀之凛然。
二聖於壯爻，與其事之善，而原其心之純焉。夫處壯莫善於貞，而中其本也。九二以之，宜二聖交發其義與！且君子之處壯，非正無以保其盛，非中無以裕其原。卦之九二，居陰失正，而所處得中。是故周公係爻，慮其有用壯之失也，而戒以「貞吉」焉。蓋大壯利貞，時則然也，故當其時者，不可以過壯也。是必以天下之公理，行天下之公事：動有關于君德，則爲之而弗過于激也；政有裨于民瘼，則爲之而弗失于驟也。觀其所發，一天地正大之情焉。惟正可以懾羣邪，而彼之伺隙乘釁者，皆不得撓吾剛動之謀矣。此正道行而吉之所以大來乎！孔子傳象，本其有得正之心也，而原其以中焉。蓋因中求正，理則然也，故事之正者，不容以襲取也。由其以天下之公道，秉天下之公心：上攄其忠，以格君之心爲心也；下宣其猷，以惠民之心爲心也。察其所存，一天地受中之懿焉。惟中可以貫萬事，而措之行
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Confucian Instructor Li: The entire essay is incisive and pertinent; reading it inspires awe.

Regarding the lines of the Great Strength (Dazhuang) hexagram, the two sages commended the goodness of its actions and traced them back to the purity of its heart. Now, in dealing with a time of great strength, nothing is better than firmness and correctness (zhen), and centrality (zhong) is its foundation. Since the Nine in the Second Place embodies this, how fitting it is that the two sages both elucidated its meaning! Moreover, when a superior man finds himself in a position of great strength, without correctness he has no means to preserve his flourishing state, and without centrality he has no means to enrich its source. The Nine in the Second Place of the hexagram occupies a yin position and thus lacks proper placement, yet where it abides attains centrality. Therefore, when the Duke of Zhou appended the line statement, he worried that it might commit the error of relying excessively on strength, and thus admonished it with "firmness and correctness bring good fortune." Indeed, that Great Strength finds advantage in firmness and correctness is dictated by the time; hence, those who face such a time must not be overly forceful. One must necessarily carry out the public affairs of the world according to the public principles of the world: if an action pertains to the ruler's virtue, one undertakes it without being overly vehement; if a policy benefits the people's sufferings, one implements it without erring in haste. Observing what is manifested, it is entirely the upright and great disposition of Heaven and Earth. Only correctness can overawe the multitude of evil-doers, so that those who watch for openings and exploit rifts are all unable to obstruct our resolute and active plans. Is this not how the right way prevails and great good fortune arrives! When Confucius wrote the Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan), he grounded it in the possession of a heart that attains correctness, and traced its source to centrality. Indeed, seeking correctness through centrality is the natural principle of things; therefore, correctness in affairs cannot be seized through outward imitation. It stems from holding fast to a public-spirited heart for the world by means of the public way of the world: above, pouring forth one's loyalty, taking the rectification of the ruler's heart as one's own heart; below, proclaiming one's plans, taking the benefiting of the people as one's own heart. Examining what is preserved within, it is entirely the admirable virtue of centrality endowed by Heaven and Earth. Only centrality can thread through the myriad affairs, so that when put into practice…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
夫何間耶今夫易之爲書也通遠邇焉塞兩間
焉人知其廣矣大矣抑孰知其原于天地乎夫
乾天也天以一氣運于上而有動靜焉靜則專
一而不貳動則直遂而不撓一專一直交而萬
物胥此乎始矣此乾之所以大也易以效天也
大不于是而生乎夫坤地也地以一氣承乎天
而有動靜焉靜則翕聚而有常動則發舒而不
匱一翕一闢交而萬物胥此乎成矣此坤之所
以廣也易以法地也廣不于是而生乎夫惟天
===
爲大而易有天道焉是天之理盡于易也而易
之大而無外者足以配乎天矣大而至于配天
則遠近上下莫有出於天者而何一之不備耶
惟地爲廣而易有地道焉是地之理盡於易也
而易之廣而無方者足以配乎地矣廣而至于
配地則遠近上下莫有出於地者而何一之不
該耶信乎易與天地準而凡變通之宜與夫陰
陽之義易簡之善皆自此而包括之矣善言易
者其亦求端于天地乎抑論天地者象形也易
punctuated: 夫何間耶？今夫《易》之爲書也，通遠邇焉，塞兩間焉，人知其廣矣、大矣，抑孰知其原于天地乎？夫乾，天也。天以一氣運于上，而有動靜焉。靜則專一而不貳，動則直遂而不撓。一專一直交，而萬物胥此乎始矣，此乾之所以大也。《易》以效天也，大不于是而生乎？夫坤，地也。地以一氣承乎天，而有動靜焉。靜則翕聚而有常，動則發舒而不匱。一翕一闢交，而萬物胥此乎成矣，此坤之所以廣也。《易》以法地也，廣不于是而生乎？夫惟天爲大，而《易》有天道焉，是天之理盡于《易》也，而《易》之大而無外者，足以配乎天矣。大而至于配天，則遠近上下莫有出於天者，而何一之不備耶？惟地爲廣，而《易》有地道焉，是地之理盡於《易》也，而《易》之廣而無方者，足以配乎地矣。廣而至于配地，則遠近上下莫有出於地者，而何一之不該耶？信乎《易》與天地準，而凡變通之宜，與夫陰陽之義、易簡之善，皆自此而包括之矣。善言《易》者，其亦求端于天地乎！抑論天地者，象形也；《易》
translation_en: …how could there be any gap between them? Now, as a book, the Changes (Yi) pervades what is far and near, and fills the space between Heaven and Earth. People know that it is vast and great, yet who knows that it originates from Heaven and Earth? Now Qian is Heaven. Heaven revolves above with a single vital force (qi), having both movement and stillness. In stillness, it is concentrated and undivided; in movement, it goes straight forward and unbent. As this concentration and straightness interact, the myriad things all take their beginning from this—and this is why Qian is great. Since the Changes emulates Heaven, does not its greatness arise from this? Now Kun is Earth. Earth receives from Heaven with a single vital force, having both movement and stillness. In stillness, it gathers in and remains constant; in movement, it unfolds and is inexhaustible. As this closing and opening interact, the myriad things all reach their completion through this—and this is why Kun is vast. Since the Changes models itself on Earth, does not its vastness arise from this? Now, only Heaven is great, and the Changes contains the Way of Heaven; thus the principles of Heaven are fully expressed in the Changes, and the boundless greatness of the Changes is sufficient to match Heaven. Being so great as to match Heaven, nothing far or near, above or below goes beyond Heaven—so what single thing is not provided for within it? Only Earth is vast, and the Changes contains the Way of Earth; thus the principles of Earth are fully expressed in the Changes, and the limitless vastness of the Changes is sufficient to match Earth. Being so vast as to match Earth, nothing far or near, above or below goes beyond Earth—so what single thing is not encompassed within it? Truly, the Changes is on a par with Heaven and Earth, and all the appropriateness of change and continuity, together with the meaning of yin and yang and the goodness of ease and simplicity, are all encompassed from this. Those who are skilled at discussing the Changes should surely seek its beginnings in Heaven and Earth! Yet if we discuss Heaven and Earth, they are images and forms; the Changes…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
者奇偶也以象形視天地則有迹矣以奇偶視
易則有文矣文者道之顯也迹者道之著也以
道而觀則象形無迹也奇偶無文也道會于吾
心也學者致吾心之廣大而天地易理以一心
而涵之矣故曰神而明之存乎其人
書
其爾典常作之師
吳懋昭
同考試官教諭單批法典守官不難措詞而鋪
敘圓融略無斧鑿是有手段者允宜高薦
考試官教諭朱批淘煉精純
考試官教授李批舂容可誦
===
賢王之訓治官惟守當代之法而已夫周之典
常法之盡善者也有治官之責者可不以是爲
師哉成王訓迪百官及此意曰王制以時爲大
臣子以趨時爲忠凡我有官君子學古而裁度
之固可以適治矣然豈但已哉我周之法創立
本於文武制作成於周公固一代之典常而入
punctuated:
者，奇偶也。以象形視天地，則有迹矣；以奇偶視《易》，則有文矣。文者，道之顯也；迹者，道之著也。以道而觀，則象形無迹也，奇偶無文也，道會于吾心也。學者致吾心之廣大，而天地《易》理以一心而涵之矣。故曰：「神而明之，存乎其人。」

《書》：「其爾典常作之師。」
吳懋昭
同考試官教諭單批：法典守官，不難措詞，而鋪敘圓融，略無斧鑿，是有手段者，允宜高薦。
考試官教諭朱批：淘煉精純。
考試官教授李批：舂容可誦。

賢王之訓治官，惟守當代之法而已。夫周之典常，法之盡善者也，有治官之責者，可不以是爲師哉？成王訓迪百官，及此意曰：王制以時爲大，臣子以趨時爲忠。凡我有官君子，學古而裁度之，固可以適治矣，然豈但已哉？我周之法，創立本於文、武，制作成於周公，固一代之典常，而入
translation_en:
… consists of odd and even lines. If one views Heaven and Earth in terms of images and forms, then there are physical traces; if one views the Book of Changes (Yi) in terms of odd and even lines, then there are written patterns. Written patterns are the manifestation of the Way; physical traces are the display of the Way. Yet if viewed from the perspective of the Way itself, images and forms have no traces, odd and even lines have no written patterns, and the Way converges within our own mind. When a scholar extends the vastness and greatness of his own mind, the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the Book of Changes are all encompassed within that single mind. Therefore it is said: "To comprehend it with spirit-like insight and illuminate it depends upon the person."

Book of Documents (Shu): "Take your constant statutes as your master."
By Wu Maozhao 吳懋昭.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Shan: On the theme of laws, statutes, and officials maintaining their duties, it is not difficult to find words; yet this exposition is seamless and harmonious, without the slightest trace of forced artifice. This is a writer of real skill, who truly deserves a high recommendation.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhu: Refined and pure.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor (jiaoshou) Li: Dignified, unhurried, and worthy of recitation.

When the worthy king instructed his governing officials, he bade them simply adhere to the laws of the reigning dynasty. Now, the constant statutes of the Zhou are laws of the utmost perfection; how could those who bear the responsibility of governing officials not take them as their master? When King Cheng 成王 instructed and guided all the officials, he touched upon this meaning, saying: Royal institutions take timeliness as paramount, and ministers and subjects take keeping pace with the times as loyalty. When all you noble men holding office study antiquity and measure your actions accordingly, you can indeed adapt to governance—yet how could it stop merely at that? The laws of our Zhou dynasty were founded at their root by King Wen 文王 and King Wu 武王, and brought to completion in their institutions by the Duke of Zhou 周公. They are truly the constant statutes of an entire era, and upon entering…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
官者所當師也爾其仰王制之昭垂而欽之焉
攸司者務守乎明徵之範思聖謨之定保而慎
之焉出令者母忘乎佑啓之方監二代而損益
法何備也于是師其法焉之綱之紀遵成憲以
攸行更三聖而經綸意何精也于是師其意焉
一弛一張奉舊章以時措為天子論思之臣燮
理寅亮其職也廟謨國體具於先世之所規畫
者其道本可繼惟善繼之而已矣為天子分猷
之臣率屬倡牧其責也吏治民瘼見於昭代之
===
所講明者其事本可述惟善述之而已矣蓋前
王之謨烈徵諸庶民即萬邦猶作孚矣況在位
之君子耶周官之法度垂諸后昆即萬世猶永
賴矣況今日之臣工耶信能以是為師則入官
者不惟學古而且師今行政者不必更化而可
善治所以敬厥職者其道得矣噫周王之訓迪
厥官其有得於制治保邦之要乎抑於是而知
成王守成之令主也自古創業之君典則所貽
至深且遠繼體者能世守而勿失雖至今存可
punctuated: 官者所當師也。爾其仰王制之昭垂而欽之焉，攸司者務守乎明徵之範；思聖謨之定保而慎之焉，出令者母忘乎佑啓之方。監二代而損益，法何備也，于是師其法焉，之綱之紀，遵成憲以攸行；更三聖而經綸，意何精也，于是師其意焉，一弛一張，奉舊章以時措。為天子論思之臣，燮理寅亮其職也，廟謨國體具於先世之所規畫者，其道本可繼，惟善繼之而已矣；為天子分猷之臣，率屬倡牧其責也，吏治民瘼見於昭代之所講明者，其事本可述，惟善述之而已矣。蓋前王之謨烈徵諸庶民，即萬邦猶作孚矣，況在位之君子耶？周官之法度垂諸后昆，即萬世猶永賴矣，況今日之臣工耶？信能以是為師，則入官者不惟學古而且師今，行政者不必更化而可善治，所以敬厥職者，其道得矣。噫！周王之訓迪厥官，其有得於制治保邦之要乎！抑於是而知成王守成之令主也。自古創業之君，典則所貽，至深且遠，繼體者能世守而勿失，雖至今存可
translation_en: …entering office should take as their model. You must look up to the luminous bequest of the royal regulations and revere them, so that those in charge of specific duties strive to observe the standards of clear verification; you must reflect upon the settled security of the sage counsels and be cautious regarding them, so that those who issue commands never forget [read 毋 for 母] the methods that assist and enlighten. Surveying the two preceding dynasties to make reductions and additions, how complete the laws are! Thereupon take their laws as your model: acting as the main ropes and smaller cords of the net, follow the established constitutions in all that you do. Passing through three sage reigns in governance and ordering, how subtle the intentions are! Thereupon take their intentions as your model: alternating between relaxation and tension, uphold the old statutes to implement them according to the times. For the ministers who deliberate and ponder on behalf of the Son of Heaven, harmonizing and reverently illuminating are their duties; since the counsels of the ancestral temple and the fundamental structure of the state are fully present in what was planned by earlier generations, their Way can inherently be continued—one need only be good at continuing it! For the ministers who share the plans on behalf of the Son of Heaven, leading subordinates and guiding the pastors of the people are their responsibilities; since administrative governance and the sufferings of the people are evident in what has been expounded by our illustrious dynasty, their affairs can inherently be transmitted—one need only be good at transmitting them! Indeed, the counsels and achievements of the former kings have been verified among the common people, so that even the myriad states place their trust in them—how much more so the noble men holding office? The laws and measures of the Zhou offices have been handed down to descendants, so that even ten thousand generations will forever rely upon them—how much more so the ministers and officials of today? If they can truly take these as their model, then those who enter office will not only study antiquity but also take the present as their teacher, and those who administer government will not need to alter the transformative teachings in order to achieve good rule; thus the Way of reverently fulfilling their duties will be attained. Ah! In instructing and guiding his officials, did not the King of Zhou grasp the essentials of regulating governance and securing the state? Moreover, from this we know that King Cheng was an admirable sovereign in preserving an accomplished heritage. Since antiquity, the canons and rules bequeathed by founding monarchs have been utmost in depth and far-reaching; if those who succeed to the body of the state can guard them from generation to generation without losing them, even down to the present day they could endure…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
矣成王繼序不忘旣以法典嚴諸巳至是又嚴
諸臣其慮淵哉雖然基命宥密祗勤于德則又
法典之本也願治者其圖之
一人有慶兆民賴之其寧惟永
金輝漢
同考試官教諭單批〔敬刑獲福勸勉之意溢于〕
〔言表他日服政必能以欽恤爲心者敬服敬服〕
考試官教諭朱批〔文思雋永〕
考試官教授李批〔格調雅馴〕
===
賢王期君民獲福之遠勉諸侯之敬刑也夫刑
者所用只資治安者也君慶民賴而極於永寧
非敬刑何以致之哉穆王訓同姓諸侯也蓋曰
人臣之典獄也所職者惟持天下之平故所用
者足綏天下之福爾能敬五刑以成三德其效
果何如耶彼上而一人以恤刑爲心者也茲則
刑措而慶集焉予政罔干樂觀化中之盛也從
欲以治坐致垂拱之休也始之奉我一人者至
是而斂福於一人矣不有慶乎下而兆民以懷
punctuated:
矣。成王繼序不忘，旣以法典嚴諸巳，至是又嚴諸臣，其慮淵哉！雖然，基命宥密，祗勤于德，則又法典之本也。願治者其圖之。

一人有慶，兆民賴之，其寧惟永。
金輝漢
同考試官教諭單批：〔敬刑獲福，勸勉之意溢于言表。他日服政，必能以欽恤爲心者，敬服，敬服。〕
考試官教諭朱批：〔文思雋永。〕
考試官教授李批：〔格調雅馴。〕

賢王期君民獲福之遠，勉諸侯之敬刑也。夫刑者，所用只資治安者也。君慶民賴而極於永寧，非敬刑何以致之哉？穆王訓同姓諸侯也，蓋曰：人臣之典獄也，所職者惟持天下之平，故所用者足綏天下之福。爾能敬五刑以成三德，其效果何如耶？彼上而一人，以恤刑爲心者也，茲則刑措而慶集焉。予政罔干，樂觀化中之盛也；從欲以治，坐致垂拱之休也。始之奉我一人者，至是而斂福於一人矣，不有慶乎？下而兆民，以懷
translation_en:
…[endure until today]. King Cheng, in succeeding to the royal line and never forgetting [his ancestors' achievements], having already held himself strictly to the laws and statutes, here also held his ministers strictly to them—how profound was his foresight! Even so, establishing the Mandate in quietude and stillness and being reverently diligent in virtue are in turn the foundation of laws and statutes. May those who desire good governance take heed of this!

"The One Man will have felicity, the millions of people will depend on him, and the peace of this state will be perpetual." [Book of Documents, "Punishments of Lü" (Lü xing)]
By Jin Huihan 金輝漢.
Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Shan 單: [The theme of revering punishments to obtain blessings and the spirit of exhortation overflow beyond the words. In the future when he takes up governance, he will surely be one who takes reverent compassion to heart—deeply admirable, deeply admirable!]
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhu 朱: [The literary thought is rich and enduring.]
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Li 李: [The style is elegant and refined.]

A worthy king anticipates the far-reaching blessings to be obtained by ruler and people, thereby exhorting the feudal lords to be reverent toward punishments. Now, punishments are employed solely to aid peace and order [reading 只 as 以]. That the ruler has felicity, the people depend on him, and this reaches the ultimate state of perpetual peace—without revering punishments, how could this be brought about? When King Mu instructed the feudal lords of the royal surname, he said in effect: When a minister is in charge of criminal cases, his duty is solely to maintain fairness throughout the realm, and therefore what he employs is sufficient to secure the blessings of the realm. If you are able to be reverent toward the Five Punishments so as to accomplish the Three Virtues, what will the effect be? Above, the One Man is he who takes compassion in punishments to heart; now, punishments are set aside and felicities gather. "When my government is not transgressed against," he delights in witnessing the flourishing of moral transformation; governing in accordance with desires, he effortlessly attains the blessings of ruling with robes hanging down and hands folded. What began as serving me, the One Man, now culminates in concentrating blessings upon the One Man—is there not felicity? Below, the millions of people are those whose lot is to be mindful of…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
刑爲分者也兹則刑清而咸賴焉民日遠罪有
所藉以全生也家用平康有所倚以立命也始
之天齊于民者至是而造福於民矣不有賴乎
君而有慶是君寧於上也民而咸賴是民寧於
下也豈特于今爲然哉太和之氣洽朝野以交
孚自衍爲永終之祜大順之風合中外以交暢
自篤爲永綏之祥繼今而爲君者非一世也深
仁所培足以爲長我王國之本則蒙成業者世
世此有慶焉宗社寧謐之祉不愈遠而有光乎
===
繼今而爲民者非一世也厚澤所被足以爲保
我黎民之基則承餘庇者世世此永賴焉海宇
寧一之休不愈久而弗替乎夫慶在一人而賴
及兆民安在一時而垂及後世敬刑成德之化
其所貽者遠矣必如是而後見曰勤之效也爾
同姓諸侯其尚欽念之哉抑刑者成也一成而
不變故君子盡心焉心者天下萬世之所繫命
也呂刑之作雖云誥四方以權宜一時之急然
一篇之中惓惓於敬刑多懼之戒其藹然惻怛
punctuated: 刑爲分者也，兹則刑清而咸賴焉：民日遠罪，有所藉以全生也；家用平康，有所倚以立命也。始之天齊于民者，至是而造福於民矣，不有賴乎？君而有慶，是君寧於上也；民而咸賴，是民寧於下也。豈特于今爲然哉？太和之氣洽朝野以交孚，自衍爲永終之祜；大順之風合中外以交暢，自篤爲永綏之祥。繼今而爲君者，非一世也，深仁所培，足以爲長我王國之本，則蒙成業者，世世此有慶焉，宗社寧謐之祉，不愈遠而有光乎？繼今而爲民者，非一世也，厚澤所被，足以爲保我黎民之基，則承餘庇者，世世此永賴焉，海宇寧一之休，不愈久而弗替乎？夫慶在一人而賴及兆民，安在一時而垂及後世，敬刑成德之化，其所貽者遠矣，必如是而後見曰勤之效也。爾同姓諸侯，其尚欽念之哉！抑刑者，成也，一成而不變，故君子盡心焉。心者，天下萬世之所繫命也。《呂刑》之作，雖云誥四方以權宜一時之急，然一篇之中，惓惓於敬刑多懼之戒，其藹然惻怛
translation_en: … punishments as their lot; now, however, punishments are clear and all rely upon them. As the people daily distance themselves from crime, they have something to depend on to preserve their lives; as households enjoy peace and tranquility, they have something to lean on to establish their destiny. What initially was Heaven regulating the people has at this point become a source of blessing for the people—is there not reliance in this? When the ruler enjoys felicity, the ruler is at peace above; when the people all rely on it, the people are at peace below. And how could this be true only of the present day? When thevitality of Supreme Harmony pervades court and countryside in mutual trust, it naturally extends into an enduring blessing; when the wind of Great Compliance unites the court and the outer realms in mutual flourishing, it naturally consolidates into an auspice of lasting tranquility. Those who succeed to the throne hereafter will not be of a single generation; what deep benevolence has nurtured suffices to serve as the foundation for prolonging our royal state, so that those who inherit the accomplished enterprise will generation after generation enjoy this felicity—will not the blessing of a peaceful and tranquil ancestral temple and altar of the soil become ever more distant in reach and more glorious? Those who follow hereafter as the people will not be of a single generation; what generous grace has covered suffices to serve as the basis for protecting our black-haired people, so that those who receive the remaining shelter will generation after generation forever rely on this—will not the excellence of a peaceful and unified realm endure ever longer without decline? Now, when felicity rests with the One Man and reliance extends to the multitudinous people, when peace exists in the present moment and is handed down to later generations, the transforming influence of revering punishments to perfect virtue leaves a legacy that reaches far indeed; only when it is like this is the efficacy of what is called diligence made manifest. May you feudal lords of the royal surname reverently bear this in mind! Moreover, punishment means completion: once completed, it cannot be altered, and therefore the superior man exhausts his mind upon it. The mind is that upon which the lives of all under Heaven for ten thousand generations depend. Although the composition of the Punishments of Lü (Lü xing) is said to have been an announcement to the four quarters as an expedient for an urgent need of the moment, throughout the entire chapter its earnest admonition to revere punishments with much fear, and its gentle, compassionate…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
之意成康忠厚之澤千載而下猶可想見矣吁
此孔子所以有取而錄之也歟
詩
禾易長畝終善且有曾孫不怒農夫克敏
曾孫之稼如茨如梁曾孫之庾如坻如
京乃求千斯倉乃求萬斯箱黍稷稻粱
農夫之慶
莫若知
同考試官教諭梁批有周以農事爲首務是作
發明上下一體之情渾見盛時氣象宜錄以式
考試官教諭朱批義意含蓄
考試官教授李批簡潔而盡
===
公卿於農事致民之力而不居其功焉甚矣公
卿之重農也下不愛其力而上不有其功其真
一體而無間者哉此詩述公卿力農奉祭而作
也意謂明君以稼穡爲務未始不以有年爲祥
然力則欲其出於民也功則惡其歸諸已也我
公卿殆有以辨此乎彼禾之弗治有秋未可必
punctuated:
之意，成、康忠厚之澤，千載而下，猶可想見矣。吁！此孔子所以有取而錄之也歟？
詩
「禾易長畝，終善且有。曾孫不怒，農夫克敏。曾孫之稼，如茨如梁。曾孫之庾，如坻如京。乃求千斯倉，乃求萬斯箱。黍稷稻粱，農夫之慶。」
莫若知
同考試官教諭梁批：有周以農事爲首務。是作發明上下一體之情，渾見盛時氣象，宜錄以式。
考試官教諭朱批：義意含蓄。
考試官教授李批：簡潔而盡。
公卿於農事，致民之力而不居其功焉。甚矣，公卿之重農也！下不愛其力，而上不有其功，其真一體而無間者哉！此詩述公卿力農奉祭而作也。意謂：明君以稼穡爲務，未始不以有年爲祥。然力則欲其出於民也，功則惡其歸諸已也。我公卿殆有以辨此乎？彼禾之弗治，有秋未可必
translation_en:
… spirit, and the loyal and generous beneficence of Kings Cheng and Kang can still be envisioned a thousand years later. Ah! Is this not why Confucius approved of it and recorded it [in the Book of Documents]?

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"The grain is well-cultivated all along the long acres; in the end it will be good and abundant. The descendant does not show anger; the husbandmen are able to be diligent. The descendant's standing grain is like thatch and like a bridge; the descendant's stacks are like islands and like mounds. He will seek a thousand granaries; he will seek ten thousand carts. Millet, panicled millet, rice, and sorghum are the blessing of the husbandmen."

Mo Ruozhi 莫若知
Associate Examiner and Instructor Liang comments: The Zhou dynasty took agriculture as its foremost task. This composition elucidates the sentiment of ruler and ruled forming a single body, fully revealing the spirit of a flourishing age. It should be recorded as a model.
Examiner and Instructor Zhu comments: The meaning and intent are richly reserved.
Examiner and Professor Li comments: Concise yet exhaustive.

In agricultural matters, the dukes and ministers bring forth the strength of the people without claiming the merit for themselves. How great indeed is the importance that the dukes and ministers attach to agriculture! Those below do not spare their strength, and those above do not claim the merit as their own—truly they form a single body without any division! This poem was composed to describe the dukes and ministers devoting themselves to agriculture in order to offer sacrifices. Its meaning is that an enlightened ruler takes sowing and reaping as his primary duty, and never fails to regard an abundant year as an auspicious sign. Yet as for the labor, he wishes it to come from the people; as for the merit, he dislikes having it attributed to himself. Do our dukes and ministers perhaps understand how to discern this? If that grain is not well tended, an autumn harvest cannot be assured…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而可無紹于此乎貽謀垂燕翼之規昭考所嘗
陟降以正內治者有家也朕今承其家旣不能
就其道矣而可無紹于此乎于是本國典之宜
昭而不愆不忘求副承辟之重守家法之明備
而以似以續克盡纘服之心一上一下頒紀法
于朝廷者憲章具在也吾其講求先王之治迹
而端冕凝旒之際一周旋而不敢忘焉一陟一
降垂彝範于宫壼者典則具存也吾其彷彿先
王之身敎而宵衣旰食之圖一步趨而不敢違
===
焉雖執競之德用爲經綸之本者不能窺其微
矣卽其所以正百官正萬民者而求之庶幾道
同于繼治不至悠遠而難及耳羣臣皆有對揚
王庭之忠者將何以助我乎雖敬勝之衷用爲
正始之原者不能探其蘊矣卽其所以脩于身
齊于家者而求之庶幾道顯于繩武不至判渙
而難合耳羣臣咸有克定厥家之責者將何以
益我乎夫道不可見則述諸事事有可紹則藉
其休成王之體道勤而咨訪至矣其纘先烈而
punctuated: 而可無紹于此乎？貽謀垂燕翼之規，昭考所嘗陟降以正內治者，有家也；朕今承其家，旣不能就其道矣，而可無紹于此乎？于是本國典之宜昭，而不愆不忘，求副承辟之重；守家法之明備，而以似以續，克盡纘服之心。一上一下，頒紀法于朝廷者，憲章具在也；吾其講求先王之治迹，而端冕凝旒之際，一周旋而不敢忘焉。一陟一降，垂彝範于宫壼者，典則具存也；吾其彷彿先王之身敎，而宵衣旰食之圖，一步趨而不敢違焉。雖執競之德用爲經綸之本者，不能窺其微矣，卽其所以正百官、正萬民者而求之，庶幾道同于繼治，不至悠遠而難及耳。羣臣皆有對揚王庭之忠者，將何以助我乎？雖敬勝之衷用爲正始之原者，不能探其蘊矣，卽其所以脩于身、齊于家者而求之，庶幾道顯于繩武，不至判渙而難合耳。羣臣咸有克定厥家之責者，將何以益我乎？夫道不可見，則述諸事；事有可紹，則藉其休。成王之體道勤，而咨訪至矣。其纘先烈而
translation_en: …and how can I fail to carry it on here? Bequeathing counsels and handing down rules to shelter and protect posterity—that through which my Glorious Father ascended and descended to rectify the internal governance was the royal household. Now that I have inherited his household, since I am already unable to reach his Way, how can I fail to carry it on here? Thereupon, grounding myself in the state statutes that ought to be made bright, without erring and without forgetting, I seek to live up to the weighty responsibility of succeeding to the sovereignty; preserving the clear and complete family laws, continuing and carrying them forward, I am able to fulfill my heart's devotion to succeeding to his work. In every ascent and descent, the regulations and laws promulgated in the court have their constitutional models fully present; I shall study and seek out the traces of the former king's governance, and while wearing the ceremonial crown with its hanging jade pendants, in every turn and movement I shall not dare to forget them. In every rising and descending, the constant norms handed down within the palace quarters have their canons and rules fully preserved; I shall emulate the personal example taught by the former king, and in my plans of dressing before dawn and eating after dusk, in every step and stride I shall not dare to violate them. Although I cannot peer into the subtleties of how his virtue of resolute strength served as the foundation of statecraft, if I seek it right in the means by which he rectified the hundred officials and rectified the myriad people, then perhaps my Way will concur in continuing his governance, and will not be so distant and far-off as to be unreachable. All the ministers have the loyalty to respond to and extol the royal court—how then will they assist me? Although I cannot fathom the depths of how his inner mind of triumphant reverence served as the source of rectifying beginnings, if I seek it right in the means by which he cultivated his person and regulated his household, then perhaps the Way will become manifest in following his footsteps, and will not be so scattered and dispersed as to be impossible to unite. All the ministers share the responsibility of being able to settle the royal household—how then will they benefit me? Now, when the Way cannot be seen, one traces it through affairs; when affairs can be carried on, one relies upon their blessings. King Cheng's embodiment of the Way was diligent, and his consultation and inquiry were utmost. That he succeeded to the meritorious achievements of his predecessors and…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎授李批跌宕不羣
春秋紀兵信而名有所繫見權之統于上也夫
權不可以下移也牡丘雞澤之役而皆統於諸
侯焉聖人繫之以名宜哉且禮樂征伐人君之
大權也權以統分分以辨名名以守禮諸侯保
有其國者恃此耳觀於桓悼之事而溴梁之盟
抑何戾哉牡丘之會齊桓以救徐合而諸侯同
次於匡矣乃率師以往救者則公孫敖與諸大
夫也聖人書曰諸侯之大夫者何蓋救灾卹患
===
征伐之權係焉次而救桓其有怠心乎然創伯
之君英明之烈尚存而七國從之以遏楚鋒以
紓徐困命由諸侯制也則夫仗鉞臨戎以為同
惡之恤者大夫特承命以從事耳孰敢奸大權
以徼寵耶經故繫以諸侯見救徐之大夫猶統
於牡丘之諸侯也雞澤之會晉悼為懼楚合而
諸侯業已同盟矣乃許成以盟陳者則叔孫豹
與諸大夫也聖人書曰諸侯之大夫者何蓋講
信脩睦禮樂之權係焉協而盟悼其有戒心乎
punctuated:
考試官敎授李批：跌宕不羣。

《春秋》紀兵信而名有所繫，見權之統于上也。夫權不可以下移也，牡丘、雞澤之役，而皆統於諸侯焉，聖人繫之以名，宜哉！且禮樂征伐，人君之大權也。權以統分，分以辨名，名以守禮，諸侯保有其國者，恃此耳。觀於桓、悼之事，而溴梁之盟抑何戾哉！牡丘之會，齊桓以救徐合，而諸侯同次於匡矣；乃率師以往救者，則公孫敖與諸大夫也。聖人書曰「諸侯之大夫」者，何？蓋救灾卹患，征伐之權係焉。次而救，桓其有怠心乎？然創伯之君，英明之烈尚存，而七國從之，以遏楚鋒，以紓徐困，命由諸侯制也。則夫仗鉞臨戎，以為同惡之恤者，大夫特承命以從事耳，孰敢奸大權以徼寵耶？經故繫以諸侯，見救徐之大夫猶統於牡丘之諸侯也。雞澤之會，晉悼為懼楚合，而諸侯業已同盟矣；乃許成以盟陳者，則叔孫豹與諸大夫也。聖人書曰「諸侯之大夫」者，何？蓋講信脩睦，禮樂之權係焉。協而盟，悼其有戒心乎？
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Confucian School Instructor Li: Bold, flowing, and extraordinary.

When the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records military operations and diplomatic pledges, the titles are attached to a specific source, showing that authority is controlled from above. Now, authority must not shift downward. In the campaigns and assemblies of Muqiu and Jize, control in both cases rested with the feudal lords; how fitting it was that the Sage attached the titles to them! Moreover, ritual, music, and punitive expeditions are the great prerogatives of a ruler. Authority governs status, status distinguishes titles, and titles preserve ritual propriety; it is solely upon this that the feudal lords rely to preserve their states. When we look at the affairs of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Dao of Jin, how perverse by contrast was the covenant at Xiuliang! At the assembly of Muqiu, Duke Huan of Qi brought the states together to rescue Xu, and the feudal lords encamped together at Kuang; yet those who actually led the troops to go to the rescue were Gongsun Ao and the various Great Officers. Why did the Sage write "the Great Officers of the feudal lords"? Because rescuing from disaster and relieving distress are matters in which the prerogative of punitive expeditions is at stake. By halting and only then sending relief, did Duke Huan perhaps harbor a slackening of resolve? Yet the heroic and enlightened vigor of the ruler who founded the hegemonship still remained, and seven states followed him to check the sharp edge of Chu and to relieve the distress of Xu—the commands were determined by the feudal lords. Thus, ingrasping the battle-axe and approaching the field of war to show compassion for a shared antipathy, the Great Officers were merely receiving commands to carry out the affair; who among them would dare to usurp great authority in order to seek favor? Therefore the Classic attaches them to the feudal lords, showing that the Great Officers who rescued Xu were still under the control of the feudal lords at Muqiu. At the assembly of Jize, Duke Dao of Jin brought the states together out of fear of Chu, and the feudal lords had already entered into a covenant together; yet those who granted peace and made a covenant with Chen were Shusun Bao and the various Great Officers. Why did the Sage write "the Great Officers of the feudal lords"? Because cultivating good faith and promoting harmony are matters in which the prerogative of ritual and music is at stake. By harmonizing and entering into a covenant, did Duke Dao perhaps harbor a cautious apprehension? …

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
然復伯之君剛明之氣方揚而八國從之以伐
楚謀以通吳好令自諸侯出也則夫刑牲歃血
以爲明神之要者大夫特奉令以共讀耳孰敢
竊大權以私交耶經亦繫以諸侯見盟陳之大
夫猶統於雞澤之諸侯也若夫溴梁之會荀偃
怒而高厚貳列侯在而諸臣盟君若贅旒大夫
張矣宜春秋特書大夫以示謹禮之意歟雖然
事常積於至微謀多忽於未兆徐之救親徃可
也而命大夫袁僑之至無盟可也而命大夫則
===
溴梁專盟謂非馴致之漸乎要之司馬司盟天
子之權出于諸侯罪也桓悼伯功去王事遠矣
於晉平又何尤焉此聖人作經必嚴王伯之辨
八月晉荀吳帥師滅陸渾之戎〔昭公十有七年〕
蔣守迪
同考試官教諭王批遷戎於内地晉與有責焉
吳滅之僅足以贖故春秋無褒貶耳是作能明
書法錄之
punctuated:
然復伯之君，剛明之氣方揚，而八國從之，以伐楚謀，以通吳好，令自諸侯出也。則夫刑牲歃血，以爲明神之要者，大夫特奉令以共讀耳，孰敢竊大權以私交耶？經亦繫以「諸侯」，見盟陳之大夫猶統於雞澤之諸侯也。若夫溴梁之會，荀偃怒而高厚貳，列侯在而諸臣盟，君若贅旒，大夫張矣。宜《春秋》特書「大夫」，以示謹禮之意歟！雖然，事常積於至微，謀多忽於未兆。徐之救，親徃可也，而命大夫；袁僑之至，無盟可也，而命大夫。則溴梁專盟，謂非馴致之漸乎？要之，司馬、司盟，天子之權，出于諸侯，罪也。桓、悼伯功，去王事遠矣，於晉平又何尤焉！此聖人作經，必嚴王、伯之辨。
八月，晉荀吳帥師滅陸渾之戎。〔昭公十有七年〕
蔣守迪
同考試官教諭王批：遷戎於内地，晉與有責焉。吳滅之，僅足以贖，故《春秋》無褒貶耳。是作能明書法，錄之。
translation_en:
Yet the ruler who was restoring the hegemony had a resolute and clear-sighted spirit that was just then rising, and eight states followed him to thwart Chu's designs and establish friendly relations with Wu; the commands issued from the feudal lords. Thus, in slaughtering the sacrificial victim and smearing its blood on the lips to form a covenant before the bright spirits, the Great Officers were merely obeying orders to read out the oath together—who among them would dare to usurp great authority for private diplomacy? The Classic therefore also attaches the words "of the feudal lords," showing that the Great Officers who covenanted with Chen were still subordinate to the feudal lords at Jize. As for the meeting atanc Xiu Liang (Xiuliang), Xun Yan 荀偃 was angry and Gao Hou 高厚 was disloyal; the feudal lords were present, yet their ministers made the covenant. The rulers were like mere appendages on a ceremonial cap, and the Great Officers had grown arrogant. Is it not fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) specially wrote "the Great Officers" to indicate the intention of carefully guarding ritual propriety? Even so, affairs often accumulate from the most minute beginnings, and plans are frequently neglected before the signs appear. In the rescue of Xu, the lords could have gone in person, yet they commanded their Great Officers to do so; upon the arrival of Yuan Qiao 袁僑, they could have dispensed with a covenant, yet they commanded their Great Officers to make one. How then can the unauthorized covenant at Xiuliang be said not to have come about by gradual development? In sum, the Marshal (Sima) and the Director of Covenants (Simeng) belonged to the authority of the Son of Heaven; for such authority to issue from the feudal lords was a transgression. The hegemonic achievements of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Dao of Jin were already far removed from true kingly governance—what further blame can be laid upon Duke Ping of Jin? This is why the Sage, in composing the Classic, strictly maintained the distinction between the true King and the Hegemon.

"In the eighth month, Xun Wu 荀吳 of Jin led a force and extinguished the Rong of Luhun." [Seventeenth year of Duke Zhao]
Jiang Shoudi 蔣守迪
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Wang 王: Jin shared the responsibility for having relocated the Rong into the interior. Xun Wu's extinguishing of them was barely enough to atone for that fault, and therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals offers neither praise nor blame. This essay clearly explains the historiographical principle of the wording; it is selected for inclusion.

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭朱批辭達氣昌
考試官教授李批格嚴語勁
春秋紀伯臣靖華之兵而平詞以示義焉夫夷
不可以亂華也荀吳於陸渾而滅之近乎義矣
春秋所以無貶與且陸渾之戎睦於楚而為中
國患久矣滅之者晉荀吳也斯與潞氏甲氏之
滅等耳春秋舉其名氏異於林父士會之書何
哉蓋以洛邑為天地之中帝王所自立也固非
裔夷之可窺王畿為都會之區臣民所歸往也
===
亦非醜類所可雜維兹陸渾本以允姓之戎徙
居伊雒之地夷夏大防蕩然潰矣有安攘之慮
者固宜滅此而後朝食也何幸晉之有是舉耶
因其貳楚而肆伐以兵既得夫執言之利數其
亂華而盡驅其族庶幾乎敵愾之師屠蒯將命
蓄謀若甚秘也然志在膺戎即有棘津之涉而
非以為詐矣祭史用牲聲威若甚震也然事在
舉義即有甘鹿之逐而非以為暴矣客容之猛
萇弘料之膚公奏於雒社華夏之氣以紓赫赫
punctuated:
考試官教諭朱批：辭達氣昌。
考試官教授李批：格嚴語勁。
《春秋》紀伯臣靖華之兵，而平詞以示義焉。夫夷不可以亂華也，荀吳於陸渾而滅之，近乎義矣，《春秋》所以無貶與！且陸渾之戎，睦於楚而為中國患久矣。滅之者，晉荀吳也，斯與潞氏、甲氏之滅等耳。《春秋》舉其名氏，異於林父、士會之書，何哉？蓋以洛邑為天地之中，帝王所自立也，固非裔夷之可窺；王畿為都會之區，臣民所歸往也，亦非醜類所可雜。維兹陸渾，本以允姓之戎，徙居伊雒之地，夷夏大防，蕩然潰矣。有安攘之慮者，固宜滅此而後朝食也，何幸晉之有是舉耶！因其貳楚而肆伐以兵，既得夫執言之利；數其亂華而盡驅其族，庶幾乎敵愾之師。屠蒯將命，蓄謀若甚秘也，然志在膺戎，即有棘津之涉，而非以為詐矣；祭史用牲，聲威若甚震也，然事在舉義，即有甘鹿之逐，而非以為暴矣。客容之猛，萇弘料之；膚公奏於雒社，華夏之氣以紓。赫赫
translation_en:
Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: The diction is expressive and thevital breath flourishing.
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: The structure is rigorous and the phrasing forceful.

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the military campaign of the hegemon's minister to pacify the central Chinese lands, using matter-of-fact wording to reveal its moral principle. Truly, the non-Chinese tribes (Yi) must not be allowed to throw the Chinese states (Hua) into disorder; in destroying the Rong of Luhun, Xun Wu came close to righteousness, and is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals makes no censure!

Moreover, the Rong of Luhun had been on friendly terms with Chu and had long been a menace to the Central States. The one who destroyed them was Xun Wu of Jin, which is on a par with the destruction of the Lu clan and the Jia clan. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals record his personal and clan names, differing from the way it recorded Xun Linfu and Shi Hui? It is because Luoyi is the center of Heaven and Earth, where emperors and kings establish themselves—certainly not a place that frontier tribes may peer upon; and the royal domain is the metropolitan region, toward which subjects and people turn in allegiance—likewise not a place where vile kinds may intermingle. Now these people of Luhun, originally Rong of the Yun surname, were relocated to dwell in the region of the Yi and Luo rivers, and the great barrier between non-Chinese and Chinese utterly collapsed. Anyone concerned with pacifying the interior and repelling the exterior ought indeed to "destroy these before eating breakfast"—how fortunate that Jin undertook this action!

Seizing upon their duplicity toward Chu to launch a full-scale military expedition, Jin gained the advantage of a just pretext; denouncing their disruption of the Chinese lands and driving out their entire tribe, Jin's forces came close to being an army animated by righteous indignation against the king's enemies. When Tu Kuai conveyed the mission, the premeditated plan seemed deeply secretive, yet because the aim was to strike the Rong, even though there was the crossing at Jijin, it was not deemed deceitful; when the ritual scribe used sacrificial victims, the display of might seemed deeply awe-inspiring, yet because the enterprise was to uphold righteousness, even though there was the pursuit at Ganlu, it was not deemed brutal. The fierceness of the visitor's demeanor was foreseen by Chang Hong; when great merit was reported at the altar of the Luo River, the spirit of the Chinese lands was relieved. Illustrious…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭許批〔題意重在征不義以明惡〕
〔此作得之宜冠多士〕
考試官教諭朱批〔詞雅瑩而意聯絡可以式〕
〔矣〕
考試官教授李批〔以古調發揮征令讀之雄〕
〔心〕
王者命將奮武而因以服乎遠焉夫遠方觀化
者也王者欲明好惡以順之得不命將而示之
武歟且聖王所以昭大順于四方者在以義正
===
天下而已故時維孟秋天地之義氣始顯王者
之義師由興乃于是有將帥之命焉以士則選
之而材官之悉具以兵則厲之而戎器之是除
桀俊之士簡練以先乎衆有功之將推誠以任
之專夫卒服習器用利而又簡能任功若此者
凡以為師出計也而其稱斯師也則謂之何亦
曰征不義而已明王之世惟民從義固無有下
殘上慢以干我天誅者一或有之不義孰甚焉
張薄伐之威而聲其罪以致討整徂征之旅而
punctuated:
同考試官教諭許批：〔題意重在征不義以明惡，此作得之，宜冠多士。〕
考試官教諭朱批：〔詞雅瑩而意聯絡，可以式矣。〕
考試官教授李批：〔以古調發揮征令，讀之雄心。〕

王者命將奮武，而因以服乎遠焉。夫遠方，觀化者也。王者欲明好惡以順之，得不命將而示之武歟？且聖王所以昭大順于四方者，在以義正天下而已。故時維孟秋，天地之義氣始顯，王者之義師由興，乃于是有將帥之命焉。以士則選之，而材官之悉具；以兵則厲之，而戎器之是除。桀俊之士，簡練以先乎衆；有功之將，推誠以任之專。夫卒服習，器用利，而又簡能任功若此者，凡以為師出計也。而其稱斯師也，則謂之何？亦曰「征不義」而已。明王之世，惟民從義，固無有下殘上慢以干我天誅者；一或有之，不義孰甚焉！張薄伐之威，而聲其罪以致討；整徂征之旅，而…
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Xu: [The thrust of the question lies in chastising the unrighteous so as to make clear what is hated. This essay grasps it and ought to top the multitude of scholars.]
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Zhu: [The diction is elegant and lustrous, and the ideas are interconnected; it may serve as a model.]
Comment by Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Li: [It expounds the command for punitive expeditions in an antique cadence; reading it stirs a heroic spirit.]

The true king commands his generals and rouses his martial might, and thereby brings distant lands into submission. Now, those in distant lands are observers of moral transformation. When the true king wishes to make clear his likes and dislikes so as to bring them into顺compliance, how could he not command his generals and display his martial might to them? Moreover, that whereby the sage king manifests great compliance throughout the four quarters lies simply in rectifying the world through righteousness. Therefore, when the season is the first month of autumn, the righteous vital energy of Heaven and Earth first becomes manifest, and the righteous army of the true king arises therefrom; thereupon, the Charge is given to the generals and commanders. As for the soldiers, he selects them so that capable officers are fully provided; as for the weapons, he sharpens them so that instruments of war are put in readiness. Outstanding and valiant men are selected and trained to take the lead before the multitude; meritorious generals are accorded sincere trust and given exclusive responsibility. Now, that the troops are well-drilled, the implements sharp and serviceable, and furthermore that the able are selected and the meritorious entrusted in this manner—all of this is planned for the marching forth of the army. And in naming this army, what is it called? It is simply called "chastising the unrighteous." In the age of an enlightened king, the people follow righteousness alone, and assuredly there are none who ruthlessly oppress those below or arrogantly defy those above so as to incur our heavenly punishment. Yet should there by chance be even one such person, what unrighteousness could be greater than this! Displaying the majesty of a punitive strike, he proclaims their crimes to carry out the chastisement; arraying the legions for the march, he…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
正其罪以脩刑是誅暴也非黷武也蓋不義之
暴天下有同惡焉王者與天下同其惡故爲天
下除其殘所惡在此所好在彼而遠方之心志
于是乎一矣是誅慢也非勤兵也蓋不義之慢
斯世有公惡焉王者與斯世公其惡故爲斯世
除其害卽所用惡知所用好而遠方之觀聽于
是乎新矣威振殊俗而畏威以効順者翕如也
孰敢有犯所惡而爲不義者乎德洽窮荒而懷
德以卽敘者忻如也孰有違所好而不慕義者
===
乎夫禁暴戢亂武之善經服遠安民王之善政
先王之因時命將也有以夫於乎兵者聖人不
得已而用之也天無所不覆王者體天之心亦
無所不愛迨暴慢之亂作雖聖人有不能自遂
其愛而征伐興焉卒之好惡明而遠方自服則
仁覆之治又無不曁是義也乃所以成其仁也
聖人豈樂于觀兵哉故天道先春而後秋王道
先仁而後義
樂者敦和率神而從天禮者別宜居鬼而
punctuated:
正其罪以脩刑。是誅暴也，非黷武也。蓋不義之暴，天下有同惡焉。王者與天下同其惡，故爲天下除其殘。所惡在此，所好在彼，而遠方之心志于是乎一矣。是誅慢也，非勤兵也。蓋不義之慢，斯世有公惡焉。王者與斯世公其惡，故爲斯世除其害。卽所用惡，知所用好，而遠方之觀聽于是乎新矣。威振殊俗，而畏威以効順者翕如也，孰敢有犯所惡而爲不義者乎？德洽窮荒，而懷德以卽敘者忻如也，孰有違所好而不慕義者乎？夫禁暴戢亂，武之善經；服遠安民，王之善政。先王之因時命將也，有以夫！於乎！兵者，聖人不得已而用之也。天無所不覆，王者體天之心，亦無所不愛。迨暴慢之亂作，雖聖人有不能自遂其愛，而征伐興焉。卒之好惡明而遠方自服，則仁覆之治又無不曁。是義也，乃所以成其仁也，聖人豈樂于觀兵哉？故天道先春而後秋，王道先仁而後義。

樂者，敦和率神而從天；禮者，別宜居鬼而
translation_en:
…rectifying their crimes to enforce punishment. This is punishing cruelty, not wantonly engaging in warfare. Indeed, the cruelty of unrighteousness is something the whole world jointly abhors. The true king shares the world's abhorrence, and thus eliminates such ruthlessness on the world's behalf. When what is abhorred lies here and what is loved lies there, the minds and wills of distant quarters are thereby unified. This is punishing insolence, not wearing out the troops. Indeed, the insolence of unrighteousness is something this age publicly abhors. The true king shares the public abhorrence of this age, and thus eliminates such harm on the age's behalf. From what he applies his abhorrence to, people know what he applies his love to, and the sights and hearings of distant quarters are thereby renewed. When majesty shakes alien customs, those who stand in awe of majesty and render obedience come together harmoniously; who then would dare offend against what is abhorred and commit unrighteousness? When virtue saturates the farthest wilderness, those who cherish virtue and take their proper places rejoice; who then would go against what is loved and fail to admire righteousness? Now, prohibiting cruelty and quelling disorder are the fine principles of martiality; subduing the distant and pacifying the people are the fine governance of kingship. That the former kings appointed generals in accordance with the season truly had its reason! Alas! Arms are an instrument that the sage uses only when he has no choice. Heaven covers all without exception; the true king embodies the heart of Heaven and likewise loves all without exception. Yet when the disorder of cruelty and insolence arises, even a sage cannot fulfill his love on his own, and so punitive expeditions are launched. In the end, when what is loved and what is abhorred are made clear and distant quarters submit of their own accord, then the governance of benevolent shelter reaches everywhere without exception. This righteousness is precisely the means by which his benevolence is brought to completion; how could the sage take pleasure in displaying arms? Therefore, the Way of Heaven puts spring first and autumn after; the Way of the True King puts benevolence first and righteousness after.

Music thickens harmony, leads the spirits, and follows Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is fitting, settles the ghosts, and…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
乎造化如此聖人法其和而樂作焉以從天者
上應乎天而平中之雅若于乾知大始有幽賛
矣法其宜而禮制焉以從地者下配乎地而儀
則之陳若于坤作成物有默相矣是禮非强制
所以配地而至序之寓于經緯者何其明且備
也樂非徒作所以應天而太和之寓于播比者
何其明且備也制作善而敦和別宜之功顯則
天地位而氣覆形載之職全陽一噓而萬物以
作以長天得其所以為天也陰一吸而萬物以
===
斂以藏地得其所以為地也向微聖人應天之
樂配地之禮疇能致之哉吁禮樂之道大矣始
之者天地終之者聖人也夫聖人胡能以禮樂
官天地耶蓋通性命可與議禮樂推位育必本
之中和惟聖人達性命之原建中和之極所以
舉禮樂而天地為昭也儀文鍾律云乎任制作
者當思其本矣
第貳場
論
punctuated:
乎造化如此。聖人法其和而樂作焉，以從天者上應乎天，而平中之雅，若于「乾知大始」有幽賛矣；法其宜而禮制焉，以從地者下配乎地，而儀則之陳，若于「坤作成物」有默相矣。是禮非强制，所以配地，而至序之寓于經緯者，何其明且備也！樂非徒作，所以應天，而太和之寓于播比者，何其明且備也！制作善而敦和、別宜之功顯，則天地位而氣覆、形載之職全。陽一噓而萬物以作以長，天得其所以為天也；陰一吸而萬物以斂以藏，地得其所以為地也。向微聖人應天之樂、配地之禮，疇能致之哉？吁！禮樂之道大矣，始之者天地，終之者聖人也。夫聖人胡能以禮樂官天地耶？蓋通性命，可與議禮樂；推位育，必本之中和。惟聖人達性命之原，建中和之極，所以舉禮樂而天地為昭也，儀文、鍾律云乎？任制作者，當思其本矣。

第貳場
論
translation_en:
… in the creative transformations of nature is like this. The sages modeled themselves on its harmony and created music; taking what follows Heaven to correspond above to Heaven, the elegance of equilibrium and centrality seems to provide mysterious assistance to "Qian knowing the great beginnings." They modeled themselves on its appropriateness and instituted rites; taking what follows Earth to match below with Earth, the setting forth of ceremonial rules seems to provide silent aid to "Kun acting to bring things to completion." Thus, rites are not arbitrarily imposed; they are that by which one matches Earth, and how bright and complete is the ultimate order residing in their warp and woof! Music is not created in vain; it is that by which one corresponds to Heaven, and how bright and complete is the supreme harmony residing in its dissemination and accompaniment! When the institutions and creations are good, and the achievements of fostering harmony and distinguishing appropriateness are made manifest, then Heaven and Earth take their proper places, and their functions of covering with vital energy and supporting with physical form are fulfilled. When yang exhales once, the myriad things thereby arise and grow—Heaven attains that by which it is Heaven. When yin inhales once, the myriad things thereby contract and are stored away—Earth attains that by which it is Earth. Had it not been for the sages' music that corresponds to Heaven and rites that match Earth, who could have brought this about?

Ah! Great indeed is the Way of rites and music! What begins it is Heaven and Earth; what completes it is the sage. Now, how is the sage able to govern the functions of Heaven and Earth through rites and music? It is because only when one comprehends human nature and destiny can one discuss rites and music with him, and to extend the realization of proper placement and nourishment, one must root it in centrality and harmony. Only the sage penetrates the source of human nature and destiny and establishes the ultimate standard of centrality and harmony. Therefore, he raises up rites and music and Heaven and Earth are made illustrious—is it merely a matter of ceremonial forms and bell-pitches? Those who bear the responsibility of instituting rites and creating music ought to reflect upon their fundamental root.

Second Session
Discourse

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
正心爲天下萬事之本
陳貴科
同考試官敎諭梁批君心萬化之原是作援證
古今根極體要末歸本心學具見忠愛惟士也
考試官敎諭朱批有議論有風骨
考試官敎授李批雅渾正大
論曰治天下有幾焉人君欲致治于天下不可
不識其幾而圖之幾者何心也人君以一身寄
之巍巍之上爲天地民物之主庶務于我乎裁
===
决家國天下于我乎觀嚮百官萬民于我乎拱
手而待命六合之內孰非吾事也苟不得其所
謂幾者而握之而欲事事而爲之理將以彌綸
天地材官萬物總人羣而成治功也不亦勞且
艱哉人君知其然是故不求治于治而求治于
心蓋誠見夫此心正否理亂關焉是天下之大
幾也幾在我而化在天下有莫知所以然者是
天下之大順也握大幾成大順則身佚而事治
上可以帝中可以王是人主之大要也正心爲
punctuated:
正心爲天下萬事之本

陳貴科

同考試官敎諭梁批：君心，萬化之原。是作援證古今，根極體要，末歸本心學，具見忠愛，惟士也。
考試官敎諭朱批：有議論，有風骨。
考試官敎授李批：雅渾正大。

論曰：治天下有幾焉。人君欲致治于天下，不可不識其幾而圖之。幾者何？心也。人君以一身寄之巍巍之上，爲天地民物之主。庶務于我乎裁决，家國天下于我乎觀嚮，百官萬民于我乎拱手而待命，六合之內，孰非吾事也？苟不得其所謂幾者而握之，而欲事事而爲之理，將以彌綸天地、材官萬物、總人羣而成治功也，不亦勞且艱哉！人君知其然，是故不求治于治，而求治于心。蓋誠見夫此心正否，理亂關焉，是天下之大幾也；幾在我而化在天下，有莫知所以然者，是天下之大順也。握大幾、成大順，則身佚而事治，上可以帝，中可以王，是人主之大要也。「正心爲…
translation_en:
"Rectifying the Mind Is the Foundation of the Myriad Affairs of the World"

Chen Guike 陳貴科

Associate Examiner and Instructor Liang comments: The ruler's mind is the source of the myriad transformations. This composition cites evidence from past and present, penetrates to the root of essentials, and in the end returns to the learning of the mind, fully demonstrating loyalty and affection—truly a scholar!
Examiner and Instructor Zhu comments: It possesses substantive argument and moral vigor.
Examiner and Instructor Li comments: Refined, profound, upright, and grand.

The discourse reads: In governing the world, there is a pivotal spring. If a ruler desires to bring about order in the world, he cannot fail to recognize this pivotal spring and attend to it. What is this pivotal spring? It is the mind. The ruler places his single person upon the lofty heights, serving as the master of Heaven, Earth, the people, and all things. The myriad affairs of state depend on him for adjudication; the family, the state, and the world look to him for direction; the hundred officials and the myriad people fold their hands before him and await his commands—within the six directions of the universe, what is not his affair? If he does not grasp what is called this pivotal spring and hold fast to it, yet desires to manage every single affair one by one—intending thereby to encompass Heaven and Earth, employ the myriad things according to their capacities, unite human society, and accomplish the achievement of good governance—would that not be toilsome and difficult indeed! The ruler knows that this is so; therefore, he does not seek order in governance itself, but seeks order in the mind. For he truly perceives that upon whether this mind is rectified or not hinges order and disorder—this is the great pivotal spring of the world; when the pivotal spring lies within oneself and transformation takes place throughout the world without anyone knowing how it happens, this is the great compliance of the world. To grasp the great pivotal spring and achieve the great compliance so that one's person is at ease while affairs are well-ordered, whereby at the highest level one can be an Emperor and at the middle level one can be a King—this is the great essential of the ruler. title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
天下萬事之本旨哉朱子之言其善干論治者
乎今夫人之一身耳聽目視手持足行四者之
不相借官也而心寔統之故心曰天君蘊之爲
性發之爲情而措之則爲事禮樂異制刑政異
施慶賞威罰異用歛之不盈一掬極之可以配
天地横四海皆是心也吾心之體廓然太公粹
然至正其初本如是而或失其體者物欲撓之
耳不觀諸水乎正錯勿動可燭鬚眉湛濁一淆
莫辨妍醜心亦若是矣故冥冥而行者見寢石
===
以爲伏虎見植木以爲後人也冥冥蔽其明也
醉者越百歩之溝以爲蹞歩之澮俯而出城門
以爲小之閨也酒亂其神也慾之撓心爲蔽爲
亂又有不可勝言者且人君尊居九重其權無
不可致凡天下之可喜可好雜然于吾前者皆
足以誘吾心而爲之蠱是故身安曲房口御五
齊命之曰損心之鴆毒耳極曼淫目備佳冶命
之曰伐心之斧斤佞幸當先宵人在側命之曰
賊心之蟊蠹人主之心關於天下甚重而攻之
punctuated: 天下萬事之本，旨哉朱子之言！其善干論治者乎！今夫人之一身，耳聽、目視、手持、足行，四者之不相借官也，而心寔統之，故心曰「天君」。蘊之爲性，發之爲情，而措之則爲事。禮樂異制，刑政異施，慶賞威罰異用，歛之不盈一掬，極之可以配天地、横四海，皆是心也。吾心之體，廓然太公，粹然至正，其初本如是；而或失其體者，物欲撓之耳。不觀諸水乎？正錯勿動，可燭鬚眉；湛濁一淆，莫辨妍醜。心亦若是矣。故冥冥而行者，見寢石以爲伏虎，見植木以爲後人也，冥冥蔽其明也；醉者越百歩之溝，以爲蹞歩之澮，俯而出城門，以爲小之閨也，酒亂其神也。慾之撓心，爲蔽爲亂，又有不可勝言者。且人君尊居九重，其權無不可致，凡天下之可喜可好雜然于吾前者，皆足以誘吾心而爲之蠱。是故身安曲房，口御五齊，命之曰「損心之鴆毒」；耳極曼淫，目備佳冶，命之曰「伐心之斧斤」；佞幸當先，宵人在側，命之曰「賊心之蟊蠹」。人主之心，關於天下甚重，而攻之…
translation_en:
… the foundation of all the myriad affairs of the world—how profound are the words of Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹]! Truly he excels at discussing governance!

Now, in a person's body, the ears hear, the eyes see, the hands hold, and the feet walk. These four do not borrow one another's functions, yet the mind truly governs them all; therefore, the mind is called the "Heavenly Ruler" (tianjun). Stored within, it is human nature; expressed outwardly, it is emotion; and put into practice, it becomes affairs. Rites and music have different institutions, punishments and administration have different applications, and rewards and penalties have different uses. Yet when gathered in, it does not fill a single handful; when extended to the utmost, it can match Heaven and Earth and span the Four Seas—all of this is the mind. The substance of our mind is vast and utterly impartial, pure and supremely upright. In its original state it is naturally like this; when it sometimes loses its substance, it is merely because material desires disturb it.

Have you not observed water? When placed level and left undisturbed, it can reflect one's beard and eyebrows; once clarity and turbidity are mixed, one cannot distinguish beauty from ugliness. The mind is just like this. Thus, one who walks in the dark sees a lying stone and takes it for a crouching tiger, or sees a standing tree and takes it for a person behind him, because the darkness obscures his vision. A drunken man leaps across a ditch a hundred paces wide, taking it for a half-pace drain, or stoops to exit a city gate, taking it for a small side-door, because wine confuses his spirit. When desires disturb the mind, causing obscuration and confusion, the effects are even more beyond description.

Moreover, the ruler dwells in exalted majesty within the ninefold palace, and there is nothing his power cannot attain. Everything in the world that is delightful and desirable congregates pell-mell before him, all sufficient to entice his mind and bewitch it. Therefore, when his person reposes in secluded chambers and his mouth partakes of the five kinds of ritual wine, these are called "deadly poisons that harm the mind." When his ears indulge to the utmost in alluring and licentious sounds and his eyes are furnished with exquisite and seductive beauties, these are called "axes and hatchets that hew down the mind." When sycophants and favorites take the lead and petty men stand at his side, these are called "root-eating and wood-boring pests that despoil the mind." The mind of the sovereign is of the utmost importance to the empire, and yet those that assail it…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
者其衆又如此若遂聽其攻而不爲制至使四
肢百骸得以役吾心而吾心爲萬化之本原者
反洸洋儻蕩莫之持檢則庶務之所取裁者何
如家國天下之所觀嚮者何如百官萬民之所
拱手待命于我者何如而顧可以是不正之心
應之乎甚哉人君之不可不正其心也君心者
表也表直而景直表枉而景枉君心者槃也槃
圓而水圓槃方而水方故採山探淵所以爲富
也上好貨則臣下百吏乘是而興利于游于田
===
所以爲適也上好逸則臣下百吏乘是而婾窳
建章甘泉所以爲觀也上好土木則臣下百吏
乘是而恠侈入海登岱所以爲奇也上好長生
則臣下百吏乘是而誕謾闢疆服遠所以爲大
也上好黷武則臣下百吏乘是而喜功興利之
人出而民力殫矣婾窳之人出而百度隳矣恠
侈之人出而天下隨風靡矣誕謾之人出而天
下爭騖于怪矣喜功之人出而大荒窮塞之外
日多事矣其幾始于一心而其流弊乃應于天
punctuated: 者，其衆又如此。若遂聽其攻而不爲制，至使四肢百骸得以役吾心，而吾心爲萬化之本原者，反洸洋儻蕩、莫之持檢，則庶務之所取裁者何如？家國天下之所觀嚮者何如？百官萬民之所拱手待命于我者何如？而顧可以是不正之心應之乎？甚哉，人君之不可不正其心也！君心者，表也，表直而景直，表枉而景枉；君心者，槃也，槃圓而水圓，槃方而水方。故採山探淵，所以爲富也；上好貨，則臣下百吏乘是而興利。于游于田，所以爲適也；上好逸，則臣下百吏乘是而婾窳。建章、甘泉，所以爲觀也；上好土木，則臣下百吏乘是而恠侈。入海登岱，所以爲奇也；上好長生，則臣下百吏乘是而誕謾。闢疆服遠，所以爲大也；上好黷武，則臣下百吏乘是而喜功。興利之人出，而民力殫矣；婾窳之人出，而百度隳矣；恠侈之人出，而天下隨風靡矣；誕謾之人出，而天下爭騖于怪矣；喜功之人出，而大荒窮塞之外日多事矣。其幾始于一心，而其流弊乃應于天
translation_en:
… [things that assail] it are as numerous as this. If one simply lets them assail it without keeping them in check, to the point that the four limbs and hundred bones are able to enslave one's mind, while one's mind—which is the fundamental source of all transformations—instead becomes unmoored and dissipated, with nothing to hold it in restraint, then what will become of the myriad affairs of state that depend on it for judgment? What will become of the family, the state, and the empire that look to it for direction? What will become of the hundred officials and the myriad people who fold their hands and await commands from us? And could one really respond to them with such an unrectified mind? Profound indeed is the necessity that a ruler must not fail to rectify his mind!

The ruler's mind is like a gnomon: when the gnomon is straight, its shadow is straight; when the gnomon is crooked, its shadow is crooked. The ruler's mind is like a basin: when the basin is round, the water is round; when the basin is square, the water is square. Therefore, mining the mountains and plumbing the depths are means of pursuing wealth; if the sovereign is fond of wealth, then his subjects and the hundred officials will take advantage of this to promote profit-seeking. Going on excursions and hunting in the fields are means of pursuing pleasure; if the sovereign is fond of ease, then his subjects and the hundred officials will take advantage of this to become indolent and slack. The Jianzhang and Ganquan palaces were built for grand spectacle; if the sovereign is fond of construction works, then his subjects and the hundred officials will take advantage of this to indulge in bizarre extravagance. Entering the sea and ascending Mount Tai were done in pursuit of the marvelous; if the sovereign is fond of immortality, then his subjects and the hundred officials will take advantage of this to engage in absurd deceptions. Expanding territory and subjugating distant lands are means of pursuing greatness; if the sovereign is fond of militarism, then his subjects and the hundred officials will take advantage of this to crave martial exploits.

When profit-seeking men emerge, the strength of the people is exhausted; when indolent and slack men emerge, all regulations and institutions fall into ruin; when bizarrely extravagant men emerge, the empire is swept along in their wake; when absurd and deceitful men emerge, the empire vies in rushing after the strange; when men who crave martial exploits emerge, beyond the great wilderness and remote frontiers troubles multiply by the day. The subtle trigger begins in a single mind, yet its resulting abuses find their response across the…

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
下吁豈不大可畏哉是故人君知吾之心不可
有嗜好也一有嗜好則天下爭以其好者中吾
之欲而吾心旣中於欲卽方寸之地渙然而莫
爲之主其所以權衡萬事而推行之者日見其
諄謬蹠盭而治愈不可幾于是乎有正心之道
焉然心之正未易言也必有洞察幾微之明而
後能正其心必有果確無難之勇而後能正其
心必有專一不貳之誠而後能正其心蓋吾之
心本公而無私也中而匪偏也正而匪邪也與
===
接爲構日以心鬭則公者鑿而私矣中正者漓
而偏而邪矣幾微之介是故宜用察也非至明
不能也黜其私以全公也克其偏以用中也祛
其邪以歸正也凜若馭馬兢若執盈非至勇不
能也廓乎公不以私間渾乎中不以偏間純乎
正不以邪間天精天粹萬物作類非至誠不能
也故宴安珍御不極口體所以防此心之毒曼
聲冶色不快耳目所以閑此心之伐佞幸宵人
屏于左右所以剔此心之蠹如是者心正貨賄
punctuated: 下。吁！豈不大可畏哉！是故人君知吾之心不可有嗜好也。一有嗜好，則天下爭以其好者中吾之欲；而吾心旣中於欲，卽方寸之地渙然而莫爲之主，其所以權衡萬事而推行之者，日見其諄謬蹠盭，而治愈不可幾。于是乎有正心之道焉。然心之正未易言也。必有洞察幾微之明，而後能正其心；必有果確無難之勇，而後能正其心；必有專一不貳之誠，而後能正其心。蓋吾之心，本公而無私也，中而匪偏也，正而匪邪也。與接爲構，日以心鬭，則公者鑿而私矣，中正者漓而偏而邪矣。幾微之介，是故宜用察也，非至明不能也。黜其私以全公也，克其偏以用中也，祛其邪以歸正也，凜若馭馬，兢若執盈，非至勇不能也。廓乎公，不以私間；渾乎中，不以偏間；純乎正，不以邪間；天精天粹，萬物作類，非至誠不能也。故宴安珍御不極口體，所以防此心之毒；曼聲冶色不快耳目，所以閑此心之伐；佞幸宵人屏于左右，所以剔此心之蠹。如是者心正。貨賄
translation_en: … the Empire. Alas! Is this not greatly to be feared? Therefore, a ruler knows that his mind must not harbor fondnesses or predilections. Once it has a predilection, the Empire will vie to cater to his desires with whatever he favors; and once his mind is struck by desire, that square inch of the heart dissolves without a master, and the means by which he weighs the myriad affairs and puts them into practice are daily seen to become perverse, erroneous, and refractory, so that good governance becomes ever more beyond reach. Thereupon arises the Way of rectifying the mind. Yet the rectification of the mind is not easy to speak of. Only when one has the discernment to penetrate subtle incipient signs can one rectify one's mind; only when one has resolute and undaunted courage can one rectify one's mind; only when one has single-minded and undivided sincerity can one rectify one's mind. For our mind is originally impartial and without selfishness, balanced and not one-sided, upright and not crooked. As it engages with external things and becomes entangled with them, struggling daily in the mind, what was impartial is chiseled away and becomes selfish, and what was balanced and upright is diluted and becomes one-sided and crooked. At the boundary of subtle incipient signs, therefore, one ought to exercise scrutiny—and without the utmost discernment, one cannot do this. Dismissing selfishness to preserve impartiality, overcoming one-sidedness to employ the mean, and dispelling crookedness to return to uprightness—trembling as if driving horses, cautious as if holding a full vessel—without the utmost courage, one cannot do this. Broadly impartial, never interrupted by selfishness; wholly balanced, never interrupted by one-sidedness; purely upright, never interrupted by crookedness; with heavenly essence and heavenly purity, becoming a model for the myriad things—without the utmost sincerity, one cannot do this. Thus, ease, comfort, and rare delicacies do not indulge the mouth and body, which is how one guards against the poison of this mind; alluring music and seductive beauty do not gratify the ears and eyes, which is how one bars the assailants of this mind; sycophantic favorites and petty men are banished from one's side, which is how one roots out the vermin of this mind. When it is like this, is the mind rectified? As for wealth, bribes, …

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
游畋懼其汨吾心也我則慎之土木長生懼其
蕩吾心也我則杜之窮兵黷武懼其暴吾心也
我則誡之如是者心正未也書史所以明此心
也吾何可廢開卷之益學問所以存此心也吾
何可替就將之勤賢人君子所以輔養此心也
吾何可乏啓沃之助而師保疑丞三公四輔日
與之稽古正學無為以守至正可也如是者心
正猶未也負扆端黻此心矣深宮燕閒亦此心
焉享帝格廟此心矣瞽御承接亦此心焉寡欲
===
以培之主靜以凝之蜎蜎蠼濩弗忘也廣廈細
旃弗肆也如是者心正吾心既正則萬事之大
本大原皆自我而握其幾矣由此以宰制天下
如戶之有樞如車之有輪將隨吾所闔闢運旋
而罔不宜者唯公也故能通天下唯中也故能
一天下唯正也故能齊天下以禮樂則脩明以
刑政則振舉以慶賞威罰則足以勸善而懲奸
由是帷帝有徽音綴衣皆常吉而宮闈正由是
藝極陳風聲樹而朝廷正由是大臣法小臣廉
punctuated: 游畋，懼其汨吾心也，我則慎之；土木長生，懼其蕩吾心也，我則杜之；窮兵黷武，懼其暴吾心也，我則誡之。如是者心正？未也。書史所以明此心也，吾何可廢開卷之益？學問所以存此心也，吾何可替就將之勤？賢人君子所以輔養此心也，吾何可乏啓沃之助？而師、保、疑、丞、三公、四輔，日與之稽古正學，無為以守至正可也。如是者心正？猶未也。負扆端黻，此心矣；深宮燕閒，亦此心焉。享帝格廟，此心矣；瞽御承接，亦此心焉。寡欲以培之，主靜以凝之，蜎蜎蠼濩弗忘也，廣廈細旃弗肆也。如是者心正。吾心既正，則萬事之大本大原，皆自我而握其幾矣。由此以宰制天下，如戶之有樞，如車之有輪，將隨吾所闔闢運旋而罔不宜者。唯公也，故能通天下；唯中也，故能一天下；唯正也，故能齊天下。以禮樂則脩明，以刑政則振舉，以慶賞威罰則足以勸善而懲奸。由是帷帝有徽音，綴衣皆常吉，而宮闈正；由是藝極陳，風聲樹，而朝廷正；由是大臣法，小臣廉，
translation_en: … and hunting excursions—fearing that they may submerge my mind, I am cautious of them; grand building projects and quests for immortality—fearing that they may unsettle my mind, I block them out; exhausting the military in wanton warfare—fearing that it may make my mind violent, I guard against it. Is the mind rectified when it is like this? Not yet. Classics and histories are the means to illuminate this mind; how could I abandon the benefits of opening a book? Learning and inquiry are the means to preserve this mind; how could I slacken in the diligence of making daily progress? Worthy men and gentlemen are the means to assist and nourish this mind; how could I go without the help of their enlightening counsel? Thus, with the Preceptor, Guardian, Doubter, Assistant, the Three Dukes, and the Four Aides, one should daily examine antiquity and rectify learning with them, practicing non-action so as to hold fast to supreme rectitude. Is the mind rectified when it is like this? Still not yet. When standing before the screen in ceremonial robes, it is this mind; when resting at leisure in the deep palace, it is also this mind. When sacrificing to the Lord on High and approaching the ancestral temple, it is this mind; when blind musicians and attendants wait upon me, it is also this mind. Cultivating it by lessening desires, consolidating it by maintaining tranquility, even in the secluded places of inchworms and loopers [in palace seclusion] one does not forget; in spacious halls on fine felt rugs one does not indulge. When it is like this, the mind is rectified. Once my mind is rectified, the great foundation and great source of the myriad affairs are all in my grasp at their subtleincipience. From this, governing and regulating the world is like a door having a pivot or a carriage having wheels: everything will follow my opening, closing, and turning without anything being improper. Only because it is impartial can it connect the whole world; only because it is balanced can it unify the whole world; only because it is upright can it order the whole world. Applied to rites and music, they are cultivated and made illustrious; applied to punishments and governance, they are invigorated and upheld; applied to rewards and penalties, they suffice to encourage the good and chastise the wicked. From this, the curtained quarters of the empress[?] have virtuous renown, the wardrobe attendants are all men of constant goodness, and the palace interior is rectified; from this, the standard of perfection is set forth, moral influence and reputation are established, and the court is rectified; from this, the great ministers abide by the law, the lesser officials are incorrupt, …

title: 萬曆四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而百官正由是智不詐愚衆不暴寡勇不苦怯
而萬民莫敢不正其有奇袤而不治者則微矣
此順之至也化之極也聖帝明王之治由此其
選也豈非正心之明驗歟當舜之世庶政乂而
黎民敏德矣乃其命禹則曰人心惟危道心惟
微惟精惟一允執厥中湯以天錫勇智表正萬
邦而仲虺所以勗之者曰懋昭大德建中于民
以義制事以禮制心夫虞商豈不稱極治哉而
其相授受相告勉尤惓惓于心學如此君人者
===
欲襲迹帝王之盛亦足以稽矣於乎斯道也乃
千聖傳心之宗旨而亦萬世言治者之準的也
然下必有格心之臣而後能進此言上必有純
心之主而後可以此言進故漢之時董仲舒甞
以對武帝矣卒無能格其多慾之蔽唐文皇弓
矢之喻若有解于正心者而不能不廑十漸之
陳識則以其心之未純故也朱子接洙泗淵源
倡明理學于有宋之季而正心誠意之說所以
爲脩齊治平之本者尤三復不置焉噫此豈直
punctuated: 而百官正；由是智不詐愚，衆不暴寡，勇不苦怯，而萬民莫敢不正。其有奇袤而不治者，則微矣。此順之至也，化之極也，聖帝明王之治，由此其選也，豈非正心之明驗歟？當舜之世，庶政乂而黎民敏德矣，乃其命禹則曰：「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一，允執厥中。」湯以天錫勇智，表正萬邦，而仲虺所以勗之者曰：「懋昭大德，建中于民，以義制事，以禮制心。」夫虞、商豈不稱極治哉？而其相授受、相告勉，尤惓惓于心學如此。君人者欲襲迹帝王之盛，亦足以稽矣。於乎！斯道也，乃千聖傳心之宗旨，而亦萬世言治者之準的也。然下必有格心之臣，而後能進此言；上必有純心之主，而後可以此言進。故漢之時，董仲舒甞以對武帝矣，卒無能格其多慾之蔽；唐文皇弓矢之喻，若有解于正心者，而不能不廑十漸之陳識，則以其心之未純故也。朱子接洙泗淵源，倡明理學于有宋之季，而正心誠意之說，所以爲脩、齊、治、平之本者，尤三復不置焉。噫！此豈直
translation_en:
…and the hundred officials are rectified; from this, the wise do not deceive the foolish, the many do not tyrannize the few, the brave do not afflict the timid, and none among the myriad people dare not be rectified. Those who remain perverse and unmanageable will be few indeed. This is the utmost of harmony and the pinnacle of transformation; the governance of sage emperors and enlightened kings takes its choice from this. Is this not clear proof of rectifying the mind?

In the age of Shun, the numerous affairs of state were well-ordered and the black-haired people were diligent in virtue; yet when he charged Yu, he said: "The human mind is precarious, the mind of the Way is subtle; be discerning, be undivided, and sincerely hold fast the Mean." Tang, endowed by Heaven with courage and wisdom, stood as a standard to rectify the myriad states, yet Zhonghui exhorted him, saying: "Strive to make illustrious your great virtue, establish the Mean among the people, regulate affairs by righteousness, and regulate the mind by propriety." Did not the Yu [Shun] and Shang dynasties represent the pinnacle of good governance? Yet in handing down the succession to one another and in counseling and encouraging one another, they were thus earnestly devoted to the learning of the mind (xinxue). For a ruler of men who wishes to follow in the footsteps of the flourishing age of those emperors and kings, this is quite sufficient for examination.

Alas! This Way is the essential principle transmitted from mind to mind by a thousand sages, and also the standard target for those who speak of governance for ten thousand generations.
